content: The thigh in humans is the region located between the pelvis and buttocks at its upper boundary and the knee at its lower boundary. From an anatomical perspective, the thigh is considered a part of the lower limb. The primary bone within the thigh is the femur, which is a single, robust, and thick bone. This strength is attributed to its high proportion of cortical bone. The femur articulates with the pelvis at the hip joint, forming a ball-and-socket joint, and with the tibia at the knee joint, forming a condylar joint. In cross-sectional anatomy, the thigh is divided into three distinct fascial compartments. These compartments are organized around the femur, which serves as the central axis, and are separated by dense connective tissue membranes known as septa. Each compartment is supplied by its own dedicated blood vessels and nerves and contains a specific group of muscles. The three fascial compartments of the thigh are: The medial fascial compartment of the thigh The posterior fascial compartment of the thigh The anterior fascial compartment of the thigh The arterial blood supply to the thigh is primarily provided by the femoral artery and the obturator arterial system. The lymphatic drainage of the thigh closely parallels the arterial pathways. The deep venous system of the thigh includes the femoral vein, the proximal segment of the popliteal vein, and several smaller veins. These veins are common sites for the development of proximal deep venous thrombosis (DVT). Additionally, the venae perforantes connect the deep venous system to the superficial venous system, which is composed of the saphenous veins. The saphenous veins are a frequent site for the formation of varicose veins. Weakness in the thigh muscles can manifest clinically as a positive Gower's sign during physical examination.
